claim: Without transposon-silencing Piwi-interacting RNAs (piRNAs), transposition causes an ovarian atrophy syndrome in Drosophila called gonadal dysgenesis (GD).
source: Without transposon-silencing Piwi-interacting RNAs (piRNAs), transposition causes an ovarian atrophy syndrome in Drosophila called gonadal dysgenesis (GD).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the relationship between piRNAs and gonadal dysgenesis in Drosophila.

claim: Harwich (Har) strains with P-elements cause severe GD in F1 daughters when Har fathers mate with mothers lacking P-element-piRNAs (i.e. ISO1 strain).
source: Harwich (Har) strains with P-elements cause severe GD in F1 daughters when Har fathers mate with mothers lacking P-element-piRNAs (i.e. ISO1 strain).
evidence: This is a direct statement about experimental observations with specific strains.

claim: Har-P is the most frequent de novo insertion in HISR-D and HISR-N lines.
source: In these lines, we discovered a highly truncated P-element variant we named 'Har-P' as the most frequent de novo insertion.
evidence: This claim is supported by sequencing data and analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: HISR-N lines lost functional P-transposase but retained Har-P's.
source: Although HISR-D lines still contain full-length P-elements, HISR-N lines lost functional P-transposase but retained Har-P's that when crossed back to P-transposase restores GD induction.
evidence: This is supported by genomic analysis and functional assays described in the manuscript.

claim: Crossing HISR-N lines back to P-transposase restores GD induction.
source: Although HISR-D lines still contain full-length P-elements, HISR-N lines lost functional P-transposase but retained Har-P's that when crossed back to P-transposase restores GD induction.
evidence: This is demonstrated through genetic crosses described in the manuscript.

claim: P-element-piRNA-directed repression on Har-P's transmitted paternally suppresses somatic transposition.
source: Finally, we uncovered P-element-piRNA-directed repression on Har-P's transmitted paternally to suppress somatic transposition.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from crosses with different P-element piRNA backgrounds.

claim: The Drosophila short Har-P's and full-length P-elements relationship parallels the MITEs/DNA-transposase in plants and SINEs/LINEs in mammals.
source: The Drosophila short Har-P's and full-length P-elements relationship parallels the MITEs/DNA-transposase in plants and SINEs/LINEs in mammals.
evidence: This is a comparative inference based on known biological systems.

claim: The sterility syndrome of 'P-M' hybrid dysgenesis in Drosophila melanogaster is due to uncontrolled P-element transposition that damages ovarian development and induces female sterility.
source: The sterility syndrome of 'P-M' hybrid dysgenesis in Drosophila melanogaster (Engels and Preston, 1979; Kidwell et al., 1977) is due to uncontrolled P-element transposition that damages ovarian development and induces female sterility (Bingham et al., 1982 and reviewed in Kelleher, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The gonadal dysgenesis (GD) phenotype occurs in hybrid F1 daughters whose paternal genome comes from a father possessing active P-elements (a 'P' strain) and a maternal genome unable to express P-element piRNAs (an 'M' strain).
source: This gonadal dysgenesis (GD) phenotype occurs in hybrid F1 daughters whose paternal genome comes from a father possessing active P-elements (a 'P' strain) and a maternal genome unable to express P-element piRNAs (an 'M' strain) (Brennecke et al., 2008; Khurana et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Daughters from the reciprocal cross are completely fertile because the mother possessing active P-elements contributes P-element-derived Piwi-interacting RNAs (piRNAs) to silence these transposons in daughters.
source: The fascinating nature of this genetic syndrome is complete fertility in daughters from the reciprocal cross because the mother possessing active P-elements contribute P-element-derived Piwi-interacting RNAs (piRNAs) to silence these transposons in daughters (Brennecke et al., 2008; Khurana et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Despite identical genetic makeup in daughters between the reciprocal crosses, the epigenetic maternal transmission of transposon repression by piRNAs starkly defines female fertility.
source: Thus, despite identical genetic makeup in daughters between the reciprocal crosses, the epigenetic maternal transmission of transposon repression by piRNAs starkly defines female fertility (illustrated in Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the illustration in Figure 1A and citations to previous research.

claim: There is a lack of correlation between P-element copy number and GD induction.
source: Thus, there is a lack of correlation between P-element copy number and GD induction (Figure 1D) that we and others have previously observed (Bergman et al., 2017; Ronsseray et al., 1989; Srivastav and Kelleher, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1D and citations to previous research.

claim: Har strain has 120-140 P-element copies.
source: Although P-element copy numbers in Har are significant (120–140 copies; Khurana et al., 2011), strains with even more copies like OreR-MOD do not induce GD whereas other strong inducer strains that have >75% fewer P-element copies than Har can also trigger complete GD (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Khurana et al., 2011 and data in Figure 1B and C.

claim: OreR-MOD strain has more P-element copies than Har but does not induce GD.
source: Although P-element copy numbers in Har are significant (120–140 copies; Khurana et al., 2011), strains with even more copies like OreR-MOD do not induce GD whereas other strong inducer strains that have >75% fewer P-element copies than Har can also trigger complete GD (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1B and C.

claim: Some strong inducer strains have >75% fewer P-element copies than Har but can still trigger complete GD.
source: Although P-element copy numbers in Har are significant (120–140 copies; Khurana et al., 2011), strains with even more copies like OreR-MOD do not induce GD whereas other strong inducer strains that have >75% fewer P-element copies than Har can also trigger complete GD (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1B and C.

claim: Very short P-element variants from the pi[2] strain assemble in vitro with the P-transposase tetramer complex >100X more efficiently than the full-length P-element.
source: In addition, there are many non-autonomous P-element variants that can be mobilized by P-transposases, including very short elements from the pi[2] strain (Bingham et al., 1982; O'Hare and Rubin, 1983) that actually assemble in vitro with the P-transposase tetramer complex >100X more efficiently than the full-length P-element (Tang et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tang et al., 2007.

claim: HISR-D lines retained severe paternally-induced GD.
source: We then subjected multiple independent Har-ISO1-Selfed-Red (HISR) lines to a second GD assay. Finally, we conducted qPCR to identify the lines with the greatest reduction of P-element copy numbers (Figure 2B) and settled on four lines each that either retained severe paternally-induced GD (HISR-D) or had lost this capacity (HISR-N) (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2B and 2C.

claim: HISR-N lines lost the capacity to induce severe paternally-induced GD.
source: We then subjected multiple independent Har-ISO1-Selfed-Red (HISR) lines to a second GD assay. Finally, we conducted qPCR to identify the lines with the greatest reduction of P-element copy numbers (Figure 2B) and settled on four lines each that either retained severe paternally-induced GD (HISR-D) or had lost this capacity (HISR-N) (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2B and 2C.

claim: HISR lines carried mostly ISO1 genomes with only a small percentage of the Har genome retained.
source: Single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) profiles of HISR lines confirmed that only a small percentage of the Har genome was retained in mostly an ISO1 background (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by SNP analysis data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: HISR-D lines produce similar-to-increased levels of P-element piRNAs compared to the parental Har strain.
source: Surprisingly, there were similar-to-increased levels of P-element piRNAs between HISR-D and Har strains, whereas amongst the HISR-N lines, only HISR-N10 retained P-element piRNAs (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by piRNA sequencing data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Among HISR-N lines, only HISR-N10 retained P-element piRNAs.
source: Surprisingly, there were similar-to-increased levels of P-element piRNAs between HISR-D and Har strains, whereas amongst the HISR-N lines, only HISR-N10 retained P-element piRNAs (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by piRNA sequencing data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: P-element piRNAs show a common 3' end antisense bias.
source: Our own mapping analysis indicated a common 3' end antisense bias of P-element piRNAs that we also confirmed with an independent piRNA analysis pipeline (Han et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by piRNA mapping analysis and citation to Han et al., 2015.

claim: All HISR-D lines and HISR-N10 are immune to strong GD induction when these females are mated to Har males.
source: These mapping patterns are consistent with piRNAs silencing transposons and suppressing hybrid GD (Brennecke et al., 2008; Erwin et al., 2015; Khurana et al., 2011) as well as correlating with all the HISR-D's and HISR-N10's immunity to strong GD induction when these females are mated to Har males (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by GD assay data shown in Figure 3D and citations to previous research.

claim: The vast majority of the P-element insertions across all HISR lines were de novo P-element insertions.
source: Surprisingly, the vast majority of the P-element insertions across all HISR lines were also de novo P-element insertions (Figure 4C), with each line clearing out nearly all parental Har P-element insertions and developing unique landscapes of P-element insertions.
evidence: This is supported by TIDAL analysis data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: During the course of stabilizing the HISR lines, there were bursts of new P-element transpositions resulting in novel transposon landscapes that are completely distinct from the parental Har genome.
source: These data suggest that during the course of stabilizing the HISR lines, there were bursts of new P-element transpositions resulting in novel transposon landscapes that are completely distinct from the parental Har genome.
evidence: This is inferred from the TIDAL analysis data showing de novo insertions.

claim: The most abundant variant accounting for more P-element copies in OreR-MOD and OreR-TK strains compared to Har were the 'KP' variant.
source: The most abundant variant accounting for more P-element copies in OreR-MOD and OreR-TK strains compared to Har were the 'KP' variant shown to encode a dominant negative protein that inhibits full-length P-transposase activity (Jackson et al., 1988; Simmons et al., 1990) (Figure 5A–5C), thus explaining the innocuous accumulation of these P-element variants in these OreR strains.
evidence: This is supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 5A-5C and citations to previous research.

claim: The KP variant encodes a dominant negative protein that inhibits full-length P-transposase activity.
source: The most abundant variant accounting for more P-element copies in OreR-MOD and OreR-TK strains compared to Har were the 'KP' variant shown to encode a dominant negative protein that inhibits full-length P-transposase activity (Jackson et al., 1988; Simmons et al., 1990) (Figure 5A–5C), thus explaining the innocuous accumulation of these P-element variants in these OreR strains.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Jackson et al., 1988 and Simmons et al., 1990.

claim: Short ~630 bp P-element variants were sequenced that were all very similar in configuration in Har, pi[2], and Birm strains, which only retains ~130 bp of the 5' end and ~500 bp of the 3' end of the P-element.
source: Interestingly, we sequenced short ~630 bp P-element variants that were all very similar in configuration in Har, pi[2], and Birm strains, which only retains ~130 bp of the 5' end and ~500 bp of the 3' end of the P-element (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: In all HISR-D lines that retain strong GD induction, the short P-element variant and the full-length P-element encoding P-transposase were detected.
source: In all HISR-D lines that retain strong GD induction, we detected this short P-element variant and the full-length P-element encoding P-transposase, whereas the HISR-N lines retained the short variant but appeared to have lost the full-length P-element (Figure 5A, right panel).
evidence: This is supported by PCR and sequencing data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: HISR-N lines retained the short variant but appeared to have lost the full-length P-element.
source: In all HISR-D lines that retain strong GD induction, we detected this short P-element variant and the full-length P-element encoding P-transposase, whereas the HISR-N lines retained the short variant but appeared to have lost the full-length P-element (Figure 5A, right panel).
evidence: This is supported by PCR and sequencing data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The majority of P-element insertions (~55–95%) in HISR-N lines were de novo short P-element insertions.
source: With the smaller number of TIDAL-predicted P-element insertions in HISR-N lines, we confirmed by locus-specific PCR the absence of full-length P-elements and that the majority of P-element insertions (~55–95%) were these de novo short P-element insertions (Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by locus-specific PCR data shown in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The strains RAL-42 and RAL-377 that cause severe GD despite having a fraction of the load of P-elements as Har also possessed Har-P-like short variants.
source: Indeed, the strains RAL-42 and RAL-377 that cause severe GD despite having a fraction of the load of P-elements as Har also possessed Har-P-like short variants (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Two P-element-containing strains RAL-508 and RAL-855 did not induce GD because only the longer KP-like elements were present.
source: Meanwhile, two other P-element-containing strains RAL-508 and RAL-855 did not induce GD because only the longer KP-like elements were present (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: GD induction was only restored in the F1 daughters of crosses between H{CP}3 females and males with many Har-P copies.
source: To test this hypothesis, we used negative-control yw-background females that lack P-transposase and transgenic H{CP}3 females that only express P-transposase in the germline (Simmons et al., 2002b) in crosses with males that either lack Har-P copies (ISO1, Lerik-P, OreR-MOD) or contain many Har-P copies (Har, HISR-N's, Birm)(Figure 6A). GD induction was only restored in the F1 daughters of this cross in strains with many Har-Ps (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by GD assay data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The KP-length and full-length P-elements in OreR-MOD and Lerik-P, respectively, did not restore GD.
source: Notably, the KP-length and full-length P-elements in OreR-MOD and Lerik-P, respectively, did not restore GD (Figure 6B, right most bars of left graph).
evidence: This is supported by GD assay data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: P-transposase acts upon Har-P loci rather than longer P-element variants to induce GD.
source: These results suggest P-transposase act upon Har-P loci rather than longer P-element variants to induce GD and support the observation for Har-P loci making up the majority of the de novo P-element insertions in HISR-N lines (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is inferred from the genetic cross data shown in Figure 6B and C.

claim: IVS3 intron splicing was the main alteration that increased P-element expression in ovaries from a dysgenic cross between Har and ISO1.
source: We also confirmed that IVS3 intron splicing was the main alteration that increased P-element expression in ovaries from a dysgenic cross between Har and ISO1, whereas Open Reading Frame (ORF) parts of the P-element transcript are only modestly increased (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Total P-element copy numbers were stable across ovaries of daughters from two sets of dysgenic and non-dysgenic crosses.
source: By using digital droplet PCR to precisely quantity total P-element copy numbers, we confirmed that total P-element copy numbers were stable across ovaries of daughters from two sets of dysgenic and non-dysgenic crosses (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by digital droplet PCR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Crosses between two different delta[2-3] female strains and males of HISR-N17, -N25, and -N31 resulted in extensive pupal lethality.
source: When we crossed two different delta[2-3] female strains to males of HISR-N17, -N25, and -N31 which lack P-element piRNA expression but have Har-Ps, we were unable to assay GD because of extensive pupal lethality (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by pupal lethality assay data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Extensive pupal lethality was confirmed in crosses between delta[2-3] and the Birm strain.
source: We also confirmed extensive pupal lethality in crosses between delta[2-3] and the Birm strain (Figure 7A) as previously described (Engels et al., 1987; Simmons et al., 1987).
evidence: This is supported by pupal lethality assay data shown in Figure 7A and citations to previous research.

claim: Somatically expressed P-transposase acting only on the Har-Ps in Birm, HISR-N17, -N25, and -N31 is sufficient to disrupt pupal development.
source: Since we also detected very short P variants in Birm that are similar to Har-P (Figure 5A and B) we conclude that somatically expressed P-transposase acting only on the Har-Ps in Birm, HISR-N17, -N25, and -N31 is sufficient to disrupt pupal development.
evidence: This is inferred from the pupal lethality data and sequencing data.

claim: The pupal lethality was suppressed when delta[2-3] females were crossed with Har-P-containing males that also expressed P-element piRNAs.
source: Unexpectedly, the pupal lethality was suppressed when delta[2-3] females were crossed with Har-P-containing males that also expressed P-element piRNAs, such as Har, pi[2], the four HISR-D lines, and HISR-N10 (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by pupal lethality assay data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Adult females of Har and HISR-N10 hybrids with delta[2-3] still exhibited severe GD.
source: These hybrid F1 progeny developed into adults, but the adult females of Har and HISR-N10 hybrids with delta[2-3] still exhibited severe GD (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by GD assay data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Severe pupal lethality was observed when delta[2-3] females were crossed to RAL-42 but not RAL-377.
source: In addition, we also observed severe pupal lethality when delta[2-3] females were crossed to RAL-42 but not RAL-377, although strong GD was still observed with RAL-377 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by pupal lethality and GD assay data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: P-element piRNAs impart a paternally-transmitted imprint on Har-P loci that resists mobilization with somatically-expressed P-transposase and enables development to adulthood.
source: These RAL strains of independent origin from Har, pi[2], and HISR lines provide convincing support for the conclusion that P-element piRNAs impart a paternally-transmitted imprint on Har-P loci that resists mobilization with somatically-expressed P-transposase and enables development to adulthood.
evidence: This is inferred from the pupal lethality suppression data with different strains.

claim: The paternally-transmitted imprint on Har-P loci is either erased in ovaries or insufficient to prevent ovarian GD.
source: However, this imprint is either erased in ovaries or insufficient to prevent ovarian GD.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that GD still occurs in ovaries despite pupal lethality suppression.

claim: The P-element piRNA pattern of HISR-N10 perfectly matches the Har-P structure since many internal piRNAs are absent.
source: Finally, the notable P-element piRNA pattern of HISR-N10 perfectly matches the Har-P structure since many internal piRNAs are absent (Figure 3B), but overall P-element piRNAs in HISR-N10 are equivalent to Har and HISR-D lines (Figure 3C), and therefore are sufficient to repress Har-P's epigenetically from being mobilized in the soma by the delta[2-3] P-transposase.
evidence: This is supported by piRNA sequencing data shown in Figure 3B and 3C.

claim: Overall P-element piRNAs in HISR-N10 are equivalent to Har and HISR-D lines.
source: Finally, the notable P-element piRNA pattern of HISR-N10 perfectly matches the Har-P structure since many internal piRNAs are absent (Figure 3B), but overall P-element piRNAs in HISR-N10 are equivalent to Har and HISR-D lines (Figure 3C), and therefore are sufficient to repress Har-P's epigenetically from being mobilized in the soma by the delta[2-3] P-transposase.
evidence: This is supported by piRNA sequencing data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: P-element piRNAs in HISR-N10 are sufficient to repress Har-P's epigenetically from being mobilized in the soma by the delta[2-3] P-transposase.
source: Finally, the notable P-element piRNA pattern of HISR-N10 perfectly matches the Har-P structure since many internal piRNAs are absent (Figure 3B), but overall P-element piRNAs in HISR-N10 are equivalent to Har and HISR-D lines (Figure 3C), and therefore are sufficient to repress Har-P's epigenetically from being mobilized in the soma by the delta[2-3] P-transposase.
evidence: This is inferred from the pupal lethality suppression data.

claim: When a P-element truncates to a ~630 bp Har-P variant, this non-autonomous variant dominates as the main mobilizing P-element during a dysgenic cross to induce strong GD.
source: When a P-element truncates to a ~630 bp Har-P variant, this non-autonomous variant dominates as the main mobilizing P-element during a dysgenic cross to induce strong GD.
evidence: This is the main conclusion inferred from all the experimental data presented.

claim: A chromatin mark resisting P-transposase activity is more likely than somatic piRNAs or siRNAs silencing the delta[2-3] P-transposase in pupal lethality crosses.
source: Although our future goal will be to determine which specific epigenetic marks are deposited at full length P-elements and Har-P's by piRNAs, we believe a chromatin mark resisting P-transposase activity is more likely than somatic piRNAs or siRNAs (Chung et al., 2008; Ghildiyal et al., 2008; Kawamura et al., 2008) silencing the delta[2-3] P-transposase in our pupal lethality crosses because we confirmed robust P-transposase mRNA expression regardless of the expression of P-element piRNAs (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is inferred from RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2A and citations to previous research.

claim: Robust P-transposase mRNA expression was confirmed regardless of the expression of P-element piRNAs.
source: Although our future goal will be to determine which specific epigenetic marks are deposited at full length P-elements and Har-P's by piRNAs, we believe a chromatin mark resisting P-transposase activity is more likely than somatic piRNAs or siRNAs (Chung et al., 2008; Ghildiyal et al., 2008; Kawamura et al., 2008) silencing the delta[2-3] P-transposase in our pupal lethality crosses because we confirmed robust P-transposase mRNA expression regardless of the expression of P-element piRNAs (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2A.

claim: In addition to copy number, genomic location may also influence host tolerance of Har-P's.
source: However, in addition to copy number, genomic location may also influence host tolerance of Har-P's, because we observed a significant rescue of viable pupae in crosses between delta[2-3] P-transposase and a derivative strain of HISR-N17 with Har-P's only on Chromosome 3 with six P-elements, while no pupae survived with delta[2-3] P-transposase and Har-P's on Chromosome 2 with nine P-elements (Figure 7—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by pupal lethality assay data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The Drosophila P-element system of hybrid GD mainly affects female sterility and requires maternally contributed P-element piRNAs to propagate transgenerational P-element silencing in daughters via trimethylation of histone H3 lysine 9 (H3K9me3).
source: The Drosophila P-element system of hybrid GD mainly affects female sterility and requires maternally contributed P-element piRNAs to propagate transgenerational P-element silencing in daughters via trimethylation of histone H3 lysine 9 (H3K9me3) (Josse et al., 2007; Le Thomas et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Sons from dysgenic crosses are fertile despite presumed somatic P-element excision.
source: Although previous studies of dysgenic crosses focused on complete GD in females (Bingham et al., 1982; Brennecke et al., 2008; Khurana et al., 2011; Rubin et al., 1982), sons respond differently because they are fertile despite presumed somatic P-element excision (Wei et al., 1991).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Mouse piRNAs bound by MIWI2 direct the re-establishment of DNA methylation marks on transposons like L1 and IAP.
source: Mouse piRNAs bound by MIWI2 direct the re-establishment of DNA methylation marks on transposons like L1 and IAP (Aravin et al., 2008), which may propagate in sperm, but Drosophila DNA methylation is not prominent (Krauss and Reuter, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Drosophila DNA methylation is not prominent.
source: Mouse piRNAs bound by MIWI2 direct the re-establishment of DNA methylation marks on transposons like L1 and IAP (Aravin et al., 2008), which may propagate in sperm, but Drosophila DNA methylation is not prominent (Krauss and Reuter, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Krauss and Reuter, 2011.

claim: Drosophila sperm undergoes histone exchange with protamines (ProtB), with little contribution of paternal cytoplasm.
source: Similar to other metazoans, Drosophila sperm also undergoes histone exchange with protamines (ProtB), with little contribution of paternal cytoplasm (Rathke et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rathke et al., 2007.

claim: Recent data support the retention of some H3K9me3 in sperm.
source: However, recent data do support the retention of some H3K9me3 in sperm (Yamaguchi et al., 2018), which might underlie the paternal imprint of piRNA-silencing of P-elements that will be investigated further in future studies.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yamaguchi et al., 2018.

claim: The retention of H3K9me3 in sperm might underlie the paternal imprint of piRNA-silencing of P-elements.
source: However, recent data do support the retention of some H3K9me3 in sperm (Yamaguchi et al., 2018), which might underlie the paternal imprint of piRNA-silencing of P-elements that will be investigated further in future studies.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on cited research.

claim: The interplay between the truncated Har-Ps and full-length P-element DNA transposon resembles the extreme proliferation of MITEs (miniature inverted repeat transposable element) in rice scavenging other transposases to mobilize.
source: This interplay between the truncated Har-Ps and full-length P-element DNA transposon resembles other examples in nature, such as the extreme proliferation of MITEs (miniature inverted repeat transposable element) in rice scavenging other transposases to mobilize (Yang et al., 2009), and short mammalian SINEs retrotransposons taking advantage of the transposition machinery of longer LINEs, since SINEs persist in much greater numbers than their longer LINE counterparts (Hancks and Kazazian, 2012).
evidence: This is a comparative inference based on citations to previous research.

claim: Short mammalian SINEs retrotransposons take advantage of the transposition machinery of longer LINEs, since SINEs persist in much greater numbers than their longer LINE counterparts.
source: This interplay between the truncated Har-Ps and full-length P-element DNA transposon resembles other examples in nature, such as the extreme proliferation of MITEs (miniature inverted repeat transposable element) in rice scavenging other transposases to mobilize (Yang et al., 2009), and short mammalian SINEs retrotransposons taking advantage of the transposition machinery of longer LINEs, since SINEs persist in much greater numbers than their longer LINE counterparts (Hancks and Kazazian, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hancks and Kazazian, 2012.

claim: Har-Ps combined with the P-transposase trigger transposition events so efficiently to be detrimental to ovarian and pupal development.
source: However, while the full impact of MITEs and SINEs on organism development is still obscure, our study indicates that Har-Ps combined with the P-transposase to trigger transposition events so efficiently to be detrimental to ovarian and pupal development.
evidence: This is the main conclusion inferred from all the experimental data presented.

claim: The high efficiency of Har-P mobilization by P-transposase may be engineered into a new generation of transposon-based mutagenesis approaches.
source: Notwithstanding, the high efficiency of Har-P mobilization by P-transposase may also be engineered into a new generation of transposon-based mutagenesis approaches.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential future applications.
